Pilot Sample Size for a Fixed Width Confidence Interval for a Normal Mean

Source: R/seq_fwd_norm_mean.R
seq_fwd_norm_mean_pilot.Rd

Returns the number of observations to collect before the stopping rule of seq_fwd_norm_mean is checked for the first time. That procedure is the purely sequential fixed width confidence interval for the mean of a normal population with unknown variance (Mukhopadhyay and de Silva, 2009).

Usage

seq_fwd_norm_mean_pilot(d, conf_level = 0.95, m_0 = 10, gamma = 1)

Arguments

d

The half width of the confidence interval, in the units of the data: the interval reported is the sample mean plus and minus d, so its full width is \(2d\). A positive number.

conf_level

The confidence level (default 0.95).

m_0

The smallest pilot sample size allowed. A whole number of at least 2; default 10. A larger value protects against stopping too early on an unluckily small variance estimate when the target is wide (see the Details of seq_fwd_norm_mean); it costs at most m_0 observations.

gamma

Positive constant that sets how fast the pilot grows as the target narrows; see Details. Default 1.

Value

A length one integer giving the pilot sample size.

Details

If the population standard deviation \(\sigma\) were known, the sample size that gives the interval \(\bar{X}_n \pm d\) the stated confidence level would be \(n^* = z_{\alpha/2}^2 \sigma^2 / d^2\) (seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal returns it, rounded up to a whole number, for a given variance). The pilot must be chosen before anything is known about \(\sigma\), so it uses only the known constant \((z_{\alpha/2}/d)^2\): $$m = \max\{m_0,\ \lceil (z_{\alpha/2}/d)^{2/(1 + \gamma)} \rceil\}.$$ With the default \(\gamma = 1\) this is \(\max\{m_0, \lceil z_{\alpha/2}/d \rceil\}\), which grows more slowly than \(n^*\) as \(d\) shrinks. It therefore does not presume a value of \(\sigma\): a pilot equal to \(n^*\) evaluated at \(\sigma = 1\) would be far too large whenever the standard deviation is well below 1 in the units of the data.

This is the package's pilot rule. It has the form of the pilot sample size of Kelley, Darku, and Chattopadhyay (2018, Equation 21), whose full width \(\omega\) is \(2d\). It should not be read as the pilot size prescribed by Mukhopadhyay and de Silva (2009).

References

Kelley, K., Darku, F. B., & Chattopadhyay, B. (2018). Accuracy in parameter estimation for a general class of effect sizes: A sequential approach. Psychological Methods, 23(2), 226–243. doi:10.1037/met0000127

Mukhopadhyay, N., & de Silva, B. M. (2009). Sequential methods and their applications. Chapman & Hall/CRC. ISBN:9780367386535

See also

seq_fwd_norm_mean; seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal for the sample size when the variance is known.

Other seq_fwd_norm_mean: seq_fwd_norm_mean(), seq_fwd_norm_mean_optimal()

Author

Ken Kelley kkelley@nd.edu, Bhargab Chattopadhyay bhargab@iiitvadodara.ac.in

Examples

# Mean score on a 100 point exam, to within 2 points with 95% confidence
seq_fwd_norm_mean_pilot(d = 2, conf_level = 0.95)
#> [1] 10
# A narrower target calls for a larger pilot
seq_fwd_norm_mean_pilot(d = 0.1, conf_level = 0.95)
#> [1] 20
